confirmed_traps: Bool flags with secondary opts register two _Option objects that share the same `obj` and `dest` (core.py:3336-3346). So repeats have to be tracked by `obj` identity, not by spelling and not by the _Option instance. Tracking per _Option instance misses `--shout --no-shout`.
Feature switches are separate Option objects that share a dest. Keying on `dest` (which is what `state.opts` uses, parser.py:171-173) wrongly flags them as repeats.

For 'first' with a bool flag, `--no-shout --shout` must keep the const of the first occurrence. Each _Option carries its own const (parser.py:162,173), so the second _Option's process must be skipped entirely, not merely prevented from overwriting a value of the same kind.

_Option.process(value, state) never receives the spelling (parser.py:169, called at 388 and 418), so naming the second-occurrence spelling in the error means changing the signature and both call sites, in _match_long_opt and _match_short_opt.

For 'first', the repeated option's value must still be consumed from rargs. `_get_value_from_state` runs before process (parser.py:378, 413). If the skip happens before value consumption, 'b' leaks into positional args.
option-repeat-policy.integration_depth: Option.__init__ validation and to_info_dict, Option.add_to_parser (pass the policy down), _Option/_OptionParser.add_option signature, _ParsingState (a seen-objects set), and both match paths, long and short. The resilient swallowing in parse_args (parser.py:308-313) already exists and needs no change.
option-repeat-policy.likely_failure_mode: Tracking repeats per _Option instance or per dest. The first misses `--shout --no-shout`; the second flags `--upper --lower`. A second likely failure: in 'first' mode, skipping `state.order.append` inconsistently, or reporting the first spelling because the opt string isn't threaded through to process.
option-repeat-policy.hardening: Define how 'first' interacts with state.order. The skipped occurrence must still be appended to state.order, because eager processing order (`--version` repeated after `--help`) is decided from order (iter_params_for_processing). Also, `-ee` short-opt clusters must count as two occurrences, with the error naming '-e'.
option-repeat-policy.reasoning: The core is a seen-set keyed by obj plus a policy branch. The traps are real, but once the spec says 'per Option object, including secondary opts', the model only needs `id(self.obj)` in state. The spelling threading touches two call sites. Several rules exist, but they mostly reduce to one well-specified mechanism. One real trap (the shared obj across two _Options) puts this at a solid 3.

confirmed_traps: The coroutine must be driven inside `with augment_usage_errors(self), ctx:` (core.py:910-911). Running it afterwards breaks get_current_context and closes resources too early, because ctx.__exit__ closes the context when depth reaches 0 (core.py:564-568).
Detection has to look at the returned object. pass_context-style wrappers hide coroutine-function-ness.

In the nested case (a loop is already running), the sub-context created by _make_sub_context (core.py:891) gets entered and exited (and closed) by the sync `with` block before the caller awaits. The returned awaitable must re-enter ctx and augment_usage_errors around the await. The callback has to be called before you know whether it is async, because sync callbacks must behave exactly as before. So the callback is called in the sync block, and the returned coroutine is wrapped in an async function that re-enters ctx. Since the first exit already ran close() on an empty stack, resources registered during the body attach to the re-entered context. Getting this right is subtle.
Chain mode collects `sub_ctx.command.invoke(sub_ctx)` results (core.py:2083-2085). This is only correct if the loop runs in Context.invoke, which Command.invoke reaches at core.py:1414.
async-command-callbacks.integration_depth: Essentially a single function, Context.invoke, but with two distinct execution paths: no running loop (asyncio.run inside the with block) and running loop (return an awaitable that re-enters the context). Result callbacks (core.py:2023) and Group.invoke inherit the fix automatically if the change stays in Context.invoke.
async-command-callbacks.likely_failure_mode: The asyncio.run path will work. In the running-loop path, the model will most likely return the raw coroutine, or an awaitable that doesn't re-enter the sub-context. The sub-command then sees the parent context, or with_resource files are closed before the body runs. Also likely: using asyncio.get_event_loop() or another wrong running-loop detection, and leaking 'never awaited' warnings.
async-command-callbacks.reasoning: The first half (asyncio.run inside the with block, checking the returned value) is easy once spelled out. The nested-loop requirement is the real difficulty: the context must be re-entered when the awaitable is awaited, augment_usage_errors must be preserved, and sync-from-loop behaviour must stay unchanged. The spec states this, but the obvious implementation is subtly wrong, and tests can check get_current_context and resource cleanup inside the nested sub-command. Two interacting execution paths with real traps make this a 4.

confirmed_traps: os.stat follows symlinks and raises for dangling links (types.py:1176-1180), so the existence test must use os.path.lexists.
The check must come before the file_okay/dir_okay checks (types.py:1189-1204).
The dash shortcut (types.py:1169-1172) already bypasses everything, as long as the new check is placed inside `if not is_dash`.

Missed by the proposer: with resolve_path=True, os.path.realpath (types.py:1174) resolves a dangling symlink to its nonexistent target, so lexists(resolved) is False and the dangling link slips through. The rule 'check on the resolved path' conflicts with the 'dangling symlinks are rejected' rule, and the spec doesn't settle which wins.
rejected_traps: Adding the key to to_info_dict is only a trap if the model chooses to add it. The spec says not to, so it's a single explicit instruction rather than an interaction.
path-must-not-exist.integration_depth: A single method (Path.convert) plus __init__ validation. Prompt re-asking already works through existing BadParameter handling, so it needs no change.
path-must-not-exist.likely_failure_mode: Using the existing os.stat try/except as the existence test, which lets dangling symlinks through. Or checking lexists after realpath when resolve_path=True.
path-must-not-exist.hardening: Require that with resolve_path=True the dangling-symlink check runs on the original value (lexists(value)) before resolution, while the returned path is still the resolved one. And state that must_not_exist with dir_okay=False rejects an existing directory with the 'already exists' message, not 'is a directory'. This forces explicit ordering between resolution, the lexists check and the type checks.
path-must-not-exist.reasoning: One early-return branch inside convert. Every trap disappears once the spec says 'use lexists, put the check first, inside the not-dash branch'. The only genuine interaction is resolve_path versus dangling symlinks, which the proposer missed.

option-show-range-toggle.integration_depth: Option.__init__ (store the attribute), Context.__init__ (parameter plus parent inheritance), and one condition in get_help_extra. All in core.py, following an existing pattern line for line.

The error message keeps the canonical form, and a string at the option level overrides a context-level False. This mirrors show_default's str/bool dual semantics (core.py:3456-3468).
option-show-range-toggle.reasoning: This copies an existing show_default precedence pattern, in a single file, with three almost independent edits. It's easy for a small model given an explicit spec.

confirmed_traps: resolve_command must return the canonical registered key, not the alias, because the returned cmd_name becomes info_name in make_context (core.py:2052, 2072), and default_map and the envvar prefix derive from it.
format_commands computes limit from len(cmd[0]) (core.py:1995). The displayed term with ' (ci, cm)' must be used for both the row and the width.
Alias lookup must live in resolve_command/get_command so that shell completion and CommandCollection see it.

Missed: the 'canonical name' is the key the command is registered under in the group (or in a source, for CommandCollection; core.py:2173-2188), which can differ from cmd.name. Implementations that return cmd.name break groups that use add_command(cmd, name='x').
Missed: NoSuchCommand currently receives possibilities=self.commands (core.py:2111). For CommandCollection that excludes source commands, and aliases must be added to the possibilities.

Missed: the 4-step lookup order with token_normalize_func (core.py:2098-2100) must be interleaved: exact name, alias, normalized name, normalized alias. Normalizing aliases also means applying the function to each alias before comparing.
rejected_traps: The info_dict key is just an explicit omission.
command-aliases.integration_depth: Command.__init__, Group.resolve_command (lookup order, canonical name, suggestions), an alias scan over list_commands/get_command so that lazy groups and CommandCollection sources are covered, and format_commands (display term plus width). Chain and completion work automatically only if the change sits in resolve_command.
command-aliases.likely_failure_mode: Building an alias map from self.commands only, which breaks CommandCollection sources and lazy groups. Or returning cmd.name, or the alias, as cmd_name. Or getting the normalize-then-alias precedence wrong so that an alias shadows a normalized real name. Plus forgetting to put aliases in the 'Did you mean' possibilities.
command-aliases.reasoning: Several rules genuinely interact: precedence across exact, alias, normalized and normalized-alias lookups; canonical-name propagation into default_map and envvars; display width; suggestions; and CommandCollection sources. They all have to be consistent across resolve_command, get_command and format_commands. Even with a precise spec, a small model will likely miss one of them (most likely CommandCollection or the canonical key).

confirmed_traps: Empty-args path: Group.parse_args only sets _protected_args when rest is non-empty (core.py:2015-2016), so Group.invoke hits ctx.fail('Missing command.') at core.py:2034 unless the no-args branch also dispatches to the default.

no_args_is_help default comes only from invoke_without_command (core.py:1753-1754), and parse_args raises NoArgsIsHelpError for empty args (core.py:2007-2008). Both have to change, and an explicit no_args_is_help=True must still win.
Completion: _resolve_context calls resolve_command and returns early when cmd is None (shell_completion.py:714-717). If the fallback lives only in invoke, completion stops at the group.
Option-looking tokens must still go through the reparse/NoSuchCommand path at core.py:2108-2111.

MISSED: resolve_command returns args[1:] (core.py:2112). For the default fallback it must return the whole arg list, otherwise 'file.txt' is silently dropped. Copying the existing return is the obvious way to get this wrong.

MISSED: resilient_parsing. The current code skips the error branch when ctx.resilient_parsing is set (core.py:2108) and returns (None, None, ...). The default fallback has to run regardless of resilient_parsing, or completion still breaks.

MISSED: ctx.invoked_subcommand must be set to the default's name before super().invoke(ctx) in the no-args branch (cf. core.py:2050-2051), and with invoke_without_command=True the group callback must run exactly once, not once in the invoke_without_command branch and again in the dispatch branch.
subcommand_metavar default must become '[COMMAND] [ARGS]...' (core.py:1767-1770 only checks invoke_without_command).
group-default-command.integration_depth: Group.__init__ (no_args_is_help default, metavar, chain TypeError), Group.parse_args (no-args help guard), Group.invoke (empty-args branch with the invoke_without_command interplay and result callback), and Group.resolve_command (fallback that keeps the full args and works under resilient_parsing), plus decorator passthrough. Shell completion only works if the fallback is in resolve_command.
group-default-command.likely_failure_mode: Puts the fallback in resolve_command but returns args[1:] (dropping the first positional), or keeps it inside the `not ctx.resilient_parsing` guard so completion still fails. A second likely failure: the empty-args plus invoke_without_command path runs the group callback twice or gives the result callback the group's value instead of the default command's.
group-default-command.reasoning: There are four separate code paths (init defaults, parse_args, both invoke branches, resolve_command), and they interact through no_args_is_help, invoke_without_command, resilient_parsing and the result callback. The proposer missed the args[1:] slicing trap and the resilient_parsing guard, and both are easy to get wrong even with a precise spec.

confirmed_traps: Section order must be first appearance, not sorted. A dict keyed by section in insertion order handles it.
The 'Options' heading must not be written when it would be empty. The existing `if opts:` guard (core.py:1304) already does this if it is applied per section.
Iterating self.params instead of get_params(ctx) drops the help option, which is appended in get_params (core.py:1104-1108).
to_info_dict must not change (Option.to_info_dict at core.py:3211-3219).
rejected_traps: Hidden handling is close to automatic: get_help_record already returns None for hidden options, and the existing loop skips None records (core.py:1300-1302).
The 'Group options before Commands' rule needs no work: Group.format_options already calls super().format_options and then format_commands (core.py:1974-1976).
option-help-sections.integration_depth: One method (Command.format_options, core.py:1296-1306), one new Option attribute, and passthrough to help_option kwargs. Group needs no changes.
option-help-sections.likely_failure_mode: Writing 'Options' as a heading even when every option is grouped, or forgetting that help_option(help_section=...) has to reach Option.__init__ (it already does via **kwargs to option()).
option-help-sections.hardening: Require column alignment across all option sections: compute one shared first-column width (capped at write_dl's col_max=30) over every visible option in every section and pass it to each write_dl call, while the 'Positional arguments' section keeps its own width. This interacts with formatter.write_dl's measure_table/col_max logic and with the hidden/empty-section rules.
option-help-sections.reasoning: Once the order and empty-section rules are written down, this is a group-by in a single method. The existing guards already handle hidden options and empty sections.

confirmed_traps: limit is computed at core.py:1995 from the longest visible command name. It must stay global and not be recomputed per section.
Must keep using list_commands/get_command (core.py:1983-1984) rather than self.commands, or CommandCollection and lazy groups break.
Sections in first-appearance order, not sorted.
Command.to_info_dict (core.py:1080-1089) must stay unchanged.
command-help-sections.integration_depth: Command.__init__ gets a new attribute, and Group.format_commands (core.py:1978-2004) is rewritten to group rows. Nothing else changes.
command-help-sections.likely_failure_mode: Moving the limit calculation inside the per-section loop. With the spec stating that the limit is global, though, the natural refactor (compute limit once, then bucket rows) is what a model will write.
command-help-sections.hardening: Add Group(section_order=[...]): named sections in that list come first in the given order (and 'Commands' can appear in the list to change where it goes), while sections not in the list follow by first appearance. A section named in section_order but with no visible commands is still skipped.
command-help-sections.reasoning: This is a single-method change, and the main trap is spelled out in the spec. The existing structure already computes limit before building rows.

confirmed_traps: Import cycle: termui imports Abort/UsageError from exceptions (termui.py:18-19), so a top-level `from .termui import style` in exceptions.py fails. It fails loudly at import time, though, so the solver will notice and use a local import.
UsageError.show is a separate echo path (exceptions.py:87-111) and does not call ClickException.show (exceptions.py:57-65), so both need the styling.
Only the second echo in UsageError.show (exceptions.py:107-111) should be styled, not the usage+hint echo (exceptions.py:106).
rejected_traps: 'Styling is removed whenever colour is off' needs no new logic. echo already strips ANSI via should_strip_ansi(file, resolve_color_default(color)) (utils.py:330), using the color the show methods already pass.
'Styling self.message instead of format_message()' is unlikely, because both show methods already format with format_message(); the natural edit wraps that existing expression.
exception-error-style.integration_depth: Two show methods in exceptions.py, plus a class attribute and a deferred import. Colour resolution is untouched.
exception-error-style.likely_failure_mode: Styling only in ClickException.show and forgetting UsageError.show. Once the spec names both paths, that goes away.
exception-error-style.hardening: Add a separate hint_style (or a per-part dict {'error':..., 'usage':..., 'hint':...}) that the UsageError hint uses. It falls back to error_style only when hint_style is unset at every level of the MRO, and an explicit None on a subclass disables it. This forces precedence across two attributes and splitting the combined usage+hint echo at exceptions.py:106.
exception-error-style.reasoning: Attribute lookup gives the required precedence for free, and echo already handles colour stripping. The rest is two small edits.

confirmed_traps: 'auto' must not touch ctx.color. Context inherits parent.color only when its own color is None (core.py:498-502).

The env checks belong in _compat.should_strip_ansi's color-is-None branch, after the pager short-circuit (_compat.py:505-512). Putting them in resolve_color_default (globals.py:54-65) would change what CliRunner's patched should_strip_ansi sees (testing.py:505-522).
The pager writer short-circuit (hasattr(stream,'color')) has to stay ahead of the env checks.
MISSED: when stream is None the function substitutes sys.stdin (_compat.py:506-507). The env checks must also apply on that path, so they cannot be placed only in the elif branch.

MISSED: NO_COLOR beats FORCE_COLOR, and empty values count as unset. An `os.environ.get('NO_COLOR')` truthiness check gives this; a model checking `'NO_COLOR' in os.environ` gets the empty-string case wrong.
rejected_traps: 'The option must be eager or subcommands won't inherit' is wrong. Group.invoke creates the sub-context only after the parent has finished parsing and running all parameter callbacks (core.py:2052), so a non-eager callback that sets ctx.color still propagates. Eagerness only matters for `--color always --help` ordering relative to the eager help option (decorators.py:621).
color-option-and-env.integration_depth: A new decorator in decorators.py following the help_option/confirmation_option setdefault pattern (decorators.py:396-401, 619-623), a small edit to _compat.should_strip_ansi, and an export in __init__.py. utils.echo picks up the change because it calls the function at runtime (utils.py:330).
color-option-and-env.likely_failure_mode: Putting the env logic in resolve_color_default (which the spec explicitly forbids), or mapping 'auto' to False. With the precedence chain written out, a model is most likely to slip on the empty-string rule or the pager short-circuit ordering.
color-option-and-env.hardening: Make FORCE_COLOR values '0'/'false' mean force-off (treated like NO_COLOR), while other non-empty values force colour on. Also make color_option's 'auto' resolve via NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR at parse time only when the parent context's color is None, so 'auto' under a parent that has an explicit Context(color=True) keeps True. This adds a three-way env interaction and a parent-inheritance rule.
color-option-and-env.reasoning: There are several precedence rules, but the explicit-over-env order falls out of the existing color-is-None branch structure. Once the spec places the env logic in should_strip_ansi, the remaining work is a short ordered if-chain and a boilerplate decorator. One claimed trap (eagerness needed for inheritance) is wrong.

confirmed_traps: Prompt path: Option.prompt_for_value passes value_proc=lambda x: self.process_value(ctx, x) (core.py:3551). The prompt answer is a bare string, so splitting only in consume_value misses it. The split has to happen in type casting too.

Prompt values are processed twice. prompt() returns value_proc's result (termui.py:272-278), Option.consume_value returns it as the value (core.py:3678), and handle_parse_result calls process_value again (core.py:2811). The second pass gets a tuple of already-converted items, so type_cast_value must not re-split or reject non-str items. Proposer missed this.

Option.value_from_envvar splits on whitespace whenever multiple/nargs is set (core.py:3617-3623). If separator is implemented as multiple=True underneath, the env var still goes down that path unless it is overridden.
A default_map string with multiple=True and nargs==1 is not split (core.py:2555 checks only nargs != 1). type_cast_value's multiple branch then iterates the string's characters (core.py:2617-2618).
Choice.shell_complete does a plain startswith on the whole incomplete string (types.py:508-515). 'x,' therefore matches nothing until the code splits on the last separator and re-attaches the prefix.

Missed by proposer: splitting depends on the source. Command-line occurrences arrive as a list ['a,b','c'] where each element must be split. A list/tuple default must NOT be split. type_cast_value alone cannot tell these two apart, so splitting must happen per source (consume_value for COMMANDLINE) or carry extra state.
option-value-separator.integration_depth: Option.__init__/_validate (core.py:3178-3198) for the TypeError/ValueError checks and forcing multi-valued behaviour. Option.add_to_parser (append action, core.py:3325-3334). Parameter.consume_value / Option.consume_value for command-line and default_map splitting. Option.value_from_envvar. type_cast_value for strings from prompt and string defaults. make_metavar for 'TEXT[,TEXT...]'. Parameter.shell_complete for segment completion. That is 5-6 cooperating paths in core.py.
option-value-separator.likely_failure_mode: Splitting everything inside type_cast_value. That either splits list defaults that should stay intact or leaves command-line occurrences unsplit. A second likely failure is the double prompt processing: the already-converted tuple gets re-split or re-converted badly. Completion that ignores the prefix is also likely.
option-value-separator.reasoning: Each rule is clear on its own, but they conflict. 'Split command-line occurrences' and 'don't split list defaults' cannot both be met at a single convergence point. On top of that, the prompt path re-processes its own output, and the env-var path has its own split logic. A small model will probably pick one place to split and break one of these sources.

confirmed_traps: Using value truthiness instead of ctx.get_parameter_source misses `--no-json` and `--count 0`.
DEFAULT_MAP must count as not explicit. The `source < ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP` convention is visible at core.py:2797 and 3661.

The check must run after the processing loop in Command.parse_args (core.py:1374-1375). Placing it right after that loop also gives the intended ordering: missing-required and conversion errors come first, and eager --help exits first.

Missed: get_parameter_source returns None for unknown names. Comparing None < DEFAULT_MAP raises a raw TypeError rather than the spec'd TypeError naming the parameter, so name validation must happen before the comparison.
rejected_traps: The feature-switch trap mostly goes away because the spec names members by Parameter.name and get_parameter_source is keyed by name. Restoring sources after lost arbitration already happens (core.py:2841-2843).
'Running before arbitration finishes' is not a realistic risk. Arbitration finishes inside each handle_parse_result, and the natural place to insert the check is after the loop.
mutually-exclusive-params.integration_depth: A constructor argument on Command plus the decorator pass-through, and one post-loop check in Command.parse_args (core.py:1376-1386) using get_parameter_source and get_error_hint. Group.parse_args (core.py:2006) calls up through it. All of this is a single code path.
mutually-exclusive-params.likely_failure_mode: Putting the check before the loop, or after the extra-args failure in the wrong order. Or not skipping the check under resilient_parsing. Or reporting the hints in the order given on the command line instead of declaration order.
mutually-exclusive-params.hardening: Prompt suppression: if a group member was already given explicitly (COMMANDLINE/ENVIRONMENT), other members of the same group must not prompt (prompt=True/required) and count as not provided. They must also not raise MissingParameter for required=True. This makes the group state visible inside Option.consume_value's prompt branch (core.py:3672-3679) and process_value's required check (core.py:2664), and it depends on processing order (iter_params_for_processing).
mutually-exclusive-params.reasoning: With the sources and the check location written down, this is about 15 lines in one spot. The rules (explicit-source test, declaration order, first violation wins, skip under resilient parsing) are independent and easy to follow.

confirmed_traps: Mutating ctx.default_map in place leaks into context_settings or the parent. Context.__init__ assigns the dict as-is (core.py:391-399), and an inherited section is the same object as the parent's nested dict. Merging must copy recursively.

A missing file at the default path vs an explicit one: the code has to check ctx.get_parameter_source in the callback. The source is set before process_value/callback runs (core.py:2791), so this works.
It must be eager so it runs before other parameters (iter_params_for_processing). This is copied directly from help_option/version_option (decorators.py:551-553, 619-621).

Missed: when the option has no default and is not given, the callback receives None and must skip loading. The --config value itself can also come from a parent default_map (source DEFAULT_MAP), and the spec doesn't say whether a missing file is then ignored or an error.
rejected_traps: The error-prefix formatting is not really a trap. A BadParameter raised inside the callback gets param filled in by augment_usage_errors wrapped around process_value (core.py:2785-2811), so "Invalid value for '--config'" comes for free.
config-file-option.integration_depth: A new decorator in decorators.py that follows the help_option pattern, plus an export in __init__.py. All logic lives in the callback (read file, json.load, deep-merge, assign ctx.default_map). No core.py changes are needed. default_map string splitting already exists (core.py:2553-2556).
config-file-option.likely_failure_mode: A shallow merge ({**old, **new}) that replaces nested subcommand sections instead of merging them. Or deep-merging into the existing dict in place, which mutates context_settings across invocations.
config-file-option.hardening: Validate unknown keys: any top-level key that is neither a parameter name of ctx.command nor (for a Group) a subcommand name/alias raises BadParameter listing the keys in sorted order. Keys that map to a subcommand must hold objects. This requires walking ctx.command.params and Group.commands, and handling sections differently from scalar values.
config-file-option.reasoning: Once the spec says 'eager, don't use exists=True, deep-merge into a new dict, check the source', each trap becomes a single instruction. The remaining risk is getting deep-merge-without-mutation right, which is a well-known pattern.

confirmed_traps: Option.get_help_extra hardcodes default_value.name for enums (core.py:3471-3472).
termui._build_prompt uses map(str, type.choices) (termui.py:117-118), which gives 'Fmt.JSON'.
Values must be stringified for int enums. normalize_choice already does str() for non-enums (types.py:416).
Added: _build_prompt must apply only to by-value choices. Switching it to _normalized_mapping for all Choices would casefold the prompt list for case_sensitive=False and break existing prompt tests.
Added: multiple=True with a list-of-enum default goes through the list branch at core.py:3469-3470 (str(d)) and still shows 'Fmt.JSON'. The spec doesn't cover this case.
rejected_traps: The to_info_dict trap only applies if the solver adds the key on its own. The spec says to leave it unchanged.
Enum defaults and empty prompt answers need no work. prompt round-trips the default through value_proc (termui.py:265-272) into Choice.convert, which normalizes the member itself.
choice-enum-by-value.integration_depth: A constructor flag and a one-line branch in normalize_choice (types.py:416). That alone covers convert, metavar, error and missing messages, and completion. Add one branch in get_help_extra and one in _build_prompt. Three files, each change trivial.
choice-enum-by-value.likely_failure_mode: Forgetting the help-default or prompt-list path. Or making the prompt list show normalized values for every Choice, which breaks existing tests.
choice-enum-by-value.hardening: With enum_by_value=True, input may match either a member's value or its name. Value matches take precedence when one member's name equals another member's value (e.g. A='b', B='a'). Metavar, errors, completion and help still list values only. This adds precedence inside convert while the displayed set stays different from the accepted set.
choice-enum-by-value.reasoning: normalize_choice is the single funnel for nearly all behaviour, so the core change is one line. The two extra display paths are named explicitly in the spec.

confirmed_traps: make_formatter must pass the new kwargs only when help_styles is set (core.py:648-650). Otherwise custom formatter_class subclasses break.
Heading style must include the colon that write_heading appends (formatting.py:206).
help_styles must be inherited in Context.__init__, in the same way color is.
rejected_traps: The column-misalignment trap is mostly not real. measure_table already uses term_len (formatting.py:19), write_dl pads with term_len (formatting.py:255-256), and wrap_text/TextWrapper are ANSI-aware since 8.4 (formatting.py:56-60, _textwrap.py:89-154). Styling the terms before measuring aligns correctly for free.
There is no extra colour-handling work. Help and usage errors are already echoed with ctx.color (exceptions.py:105-106), so color=False strips the ANSI codes.
help-styles.integration_depth: HelpFormatter.__init__ gets two kwargs. write_heading styles f'{heading}:'. write_dl styles the first column. write_usage styles only the default prefix. Context.__init__ adds inheritance and make_formatter passes kwargs conditionally. Those are local edits in two files.
help-styles.likely_failure_mode: Always passing heading_style/term_style from make_formatter. Or styling an explicit write_usage prefix. Or missing parent inheritance when help_styles is None.
help-styles.hardening: term_style applies only to the option names in the first column, not to the metavar or separators. In '-n, --name TEXT' only '-n' and '--name' are styled; in '--shout / --no-shout' both names are styled but the ' / ' is not. This means changing Option.get_help_record/_write_opts (or passing structured terms), while alignment still uses visible width.
help-styles.reasoning: The existing ANSI-aware width infrastructure removes the main claimed trap. What's left is a handful of independent local edits that are each specified directly.

option-repeat-policy.who_benefits: Authors of CLIs with long command lines who want duplicate single-value options rejected. Probably few, and the existing workaround (multiple=True plus a length check) is simple.

user_evidence.finding: A Stack Overflow question about error on repeated argument. It appeared in search results, but I did not open it, so I cannot say whether it concerns argparse or Click.
A uv issue that appeared in search results. I did not open it. Per the search snippet, it asks for a hard error rather than last-wins, in a different tool.

contrived_rules: 'first' with a bool flag that has secondary opts must give the first occurrence's const
Counting per Option object so that feature switches sharing a dest are not repeats
on_repeat other than 'last' with multiple=True or count=True raises TypeError
Three policy values ('last', 'first', 'error') where users mostly ask for an error
option-repeat-policy.reasoning: I found no pallets/click issue asking for this. My issues search for repeated options returned an unrelated PR, and the lightrun page that was meant to cover a GitHub issue returned only a blog index. A search snippet says a 2018 community comment suggested using multiple=True and raising BadOptionUsage. That snippet is the only trace of a Click request, and I could not verify it. The 'first' policy has no stated use case. The change touches the parser internals and the option constructor, so it adds a lot of surface for little shown demand.
searches: click python option specified multiple times error last wins

async-command-callbacks.who_benefits: Developers with asyncio-based application code who write async def commands. Many hit it, and today they use a asyncio.run wrapper, safir's run_with_asyncio, or the asyncclick fork. Typer supports async commands natively.

user_evidence.finding: Open since 2021 with 23 comments. davidism said auto-starting an event loop for async def callbacks is the most plausible addition, but also doubted the need and noted that asyncio.run already works. mitsuhiko worried about recursive subcommand invocation. Users want Context.with_resource and call_on_close to be async-aware.

PR #3419 'Support async command callbacks' was closed and labeled 'rejected AI'. The page does not show maintainer reasoning, and the label may refer to the PR's AI origin. #2033 and #2360 are still open.
Safir ships a run_with_asyncio decorator, which shows downstream projects work around the gap.

contrived_rules: Returning an awaitable from ctx.invoke when a loop is already running, and re-entering the sub-context on await. This is a complex dual-mode return type that mitsuhiko's design concern points at.
async-command-callbacks.reasoning: The demand is real and long-standing, and workarounds are widespread. Maintainers are lukewarm, though: davidism wants a concrete use case and notes that asyncio.run works, and mitsuhiko raised nesting concerns, so this outline's nested-invoke design touches exactly that open question. There is no merged precedent. The idea of auto-running async callbacks has some maintainer backing, but the outline's dual sync/awaitable ctx.invoke is heavy and not something users asked for.
searches: click async def command asyncio.run decorator stackoverflow

path-must-not-exist.who_benefits: Authors of commands that create output files and want to refuse overwrites, such as init or export commands. It is a common need, but many want prompting, --force or appending instead.

user_evidence.finding: Open since 2019. davidism declined separate flags in 2020 and suggested a custom type or callback, because handling an existing file can mean append, prompt, fail or rename. He said he would prefer exists=None/True/False if it were added. jpmckinney (2024) wanted it. A contributor proposed a 'state' parameter.
LSST Data Butler subclasses click.Path as MWPath, where exists=False means the path must not exist. This is a downstream workaround.
Optique, a Node/Deno parser, has mustNotExist for output files to prevent accidental overwrites. It is a different ecosystem, so it only shows that the idea is useful elsewhere.

contrived_rules: Dangling symlinks are rejected via lexists semantics. This is reasonable, but only a few users would ask for it.

Message title-casing by type name and a separate must_not_exist flag. davidism explicitly disfavored a separate flag and wanted exists=None/True/False instead, so the API shape contradicts maintainer preference.
path-must-not-exist.reasoning: The need is evidenced and a downstream subclass exists. The maintainer's stated objection is to the API shape, since a separate boolean allows nonsensical combinations. The outline uses exactly that shape and adds a TypeError for the exists=True combination. The semantics are small and sensible, but the design conflicts with davidism's stated preference.
searches: click.Path file must not exist overwrite prevent option validation stackoverflow

option-show-range-toggle.who_benefits: Authors with IntRange or FloatRange options, such as clamped -v counters, who find the auto-shown range noisy or misleading. It is a narrow cosmetic need.

user_evidence.finding: Requested in Feb 2024 for a -v count with a clamped IntRange. davidism said 'eventually' it would be worth doing, but through a planned help-formatter refactor and not another special case. gar1t shared a workaround that subclasses IntRange and overrides the range description. The issue is still open.
The range display was added deliberately in PR #1586, merged in 2020. #2679 is the only request I found to hide it.

contrived_rules: A Context-level show_range inherited from the parent, mirroring show_default. It adds a context setting that nobody asked for, and the issue only asks for an option-level toggle.
show_range=True does not reveal the implicit count range. This is a special case.
option-show-range-toggle.reasoning: The demand is a single issue, and it has a workable workaround. The maintainer is receptive but explicitly does not want more per-feature special cases, preferring a generic mechanism that collects extras from the type. A show_range boolean on both Option and Context goes against that stated direction. It is useful for the few users it affects.
searches: click hide range IntRange help text show_range

command-aliases.who_benefits: Authors of git-like, multi-command CLIs who want short names such as ci for commit. They currently need click-aliases, click-alias, cloup, core-extensions or a custom Group subclass. Many CLIs hit this.

user_evidence.finding: click-aliases adds multiple aliases to a group or command. It has 56 stars and 20 forks.
A Stack Overflow question about giving a click group multiple names. It surfaced in search results, and I did not open it. The search snippet says the answer subclasses Group.
One of several separate PyPI packages for the same purpose (click-aliases, click-with-aliasing, click-alias, a click-hotoffthehamster variant). Cloup and core-extensions also ship alias groups.

contrived_rules: Lookup order: exact name, then aliases, then normalized name, then aliases after normalization. This is a five-step precedence that few users need.
Short-help truncation width must include the alias suffix. This is a detail, not a user request.
command-aliases.reasoning: Many independent third-party packages and a Stack Overflow question show persistent demand. The outline fixes real problems that subclasses have, such as default_map, the envvar prefix and completion all using the canonical name. I did not find a pallets/click issue, or a maintainer statement, either accepting or declining built-in aliases, so I cannot say how maintainers would see it. The examples/aliases directory suggests they treat it as a user-land pattern. I did not read the repo to confirm.
searches: click group command alias stackoverflow multiple names subcommand

group-default-command.who_benefits: Authors of CLIs with one main action plus a few admin subcommands (`tool file.txt` vs `tool run file.txt`). The need is occasional, and a third-party package already covers it.

user_evidence.finding: click-default-group does this. It has 79 stars and its README describes it as invoking a command without an explicit subcommand name.
Only loosely related issues turned up (#3059, #3100 about invoke_without_command). I found no core request for a default command.

contrived_rules: Group(chain=True, default_command=...) raises TypeError at construction (a reasonable restriction, but one the outline invented)
no_args_is_help defaults to False when default_command is set (an unusual implicit coupling)
group-default-command.reasoning: There is real, if modest, demand: a contrib package exists and is used. I found no issue asking for it in core, and the maintainers might say the contrib package is enough. The design is large and touches parse_args, invoke, resolve_command and completion. Implementing it in core is plausible, but demand is moderate.
searches: click default subcommand group invoke without subcommand name

option-help-sections.who_benefits: Authors of commands with many options (tens of flags) who want argparse-style headings in --help. Issue #373 has been open since 2015 and has 28 comments. Most CLIs with large option sets run into this.

user_evidence.finding: Open since 2015. Requests an equivalent of argparse's add_argument_group. A maintainer was unsure it belonged in core and suggested subclassing, while thedrow favoured adding chrisjsewell's `help_group` approach to core. Workarounds are cloup, click-option-group and rich-click.
121 stars. Exists because Click 'has no the functionality for creating option groups' and users asked for it in Click issues.
Related help-output issues #2437 (closed) and #1112 (closed), plus a WIP PR #3097 on low-level help customization.

contrived_rules: Trap rules about sorted vs first-appearance order, and per-section column alignment, are design choices rather than user needs (minor)
option-help-sections.reasoning: Long-standing, widely discussed request with several third-party packages built on it. The core maintainers have been ambivalent (preferring subclassing), which is a risk. A simple per-option `help_section` attribute is small and fits Click's design.

command-help-sections.who_benefits: Maintainers of CLIs with dozens of subcommands (cloup users, rich-click users). Less common than option groups, but the demand is similar.

user_evidence.finding: The thread includes a 2019 workaround for grouping subcommands into sections (jtrakk), and cloup was built for help sections.
Cloup ships subcommand sections as a headline feature. The page doesn't say which Click limitation it addresses.
#1112 (separate Group subcommands and commands in help) and #2437 (splitting help into group sections) were both closed. #373 is the only matching open issue.

contrived_rules: The short-help `limit` must be computed globally across sections (an implementation detail rather than a user need)
command-help-sections.reasoning: There is real demand, evidenced by cloup, but the specific issues about command sections were closed and the maintainers' view is that subclassing suffices. The `help_section` attribute on Command is simple. A moderate score reflects the lack of a direct core request and its overlap with option sections.
searches: click group commands into sections in help output subcommands categories

exception-error-style.who_benefits: CLI authors who want red 'Error:' output. They currently subclass ClickException and override show(). The need is occasional but the request is old and recurring.

user_evidence.finding: Open since 2018. davidism proposed calling style() on the message with style args on ClickException. A later attempt hit a circular import between termui and exceptions. Still open and no design is settled.
#944 is the open request. #2193 (ctx.color ignored in ClickException.show) was fixed. #1917 (overriding exception text) is related but different.
Example of a project subclassing ClickException with a custom show() that uses secho(fg='red'), i.e. the workaround.

contrived_rules: Only the 'Error:' line is styled while usage and hint stay unstyled (a deliberate choice rather than a user need)
exception-error-style.reasoning: The maintainer himself sketched this approach, so it fits. Evidence of demand is thin: one old issue with 6 comments and scattered override snippets. A class-level global dict attribute is somewhat unusual for Click's API. It is a modest convenience.

color-option-and-env.who_benefits: Nearly every CLI author who uses colour: users in CI (GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins) want FORCE_COLOR, and users who set NO_COLOR expect it to be honoured. The need recurs across many projects.

user_evidence.finding: Open since July 2025, labelled Feature. Asks for FORCE_COLOR and NO_COLOR support because CI logs aren't TTYs. A maintainer (kdeldycke) pointed to click-extra. #2781 was marked as a duplicate.
Closed as a duplicate of #1498 in 2022. davidism doubted NO_COLOR was an accepted standard and suggested reading it in the app and passing it to `color`. He also noted Click has no --color option.
click-extra ships a `--color` option and NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR handling because Click lacks it.
Repeated requests: #1498, #2207, #3022 and PR #3845 (rejected AI).

contrived_rules: Treating the empty string as unset is sensible, not contrived
Precedence between NO_COLOR and FORCE_COLOR (NO_COLOR wins) is a choice that other tools make differently
color-option-and-env.reasoning: The most frequently requested of the five, with several issues over years and a current open one. Earlier requests were closed, with the maintainer's reasoning being that the standard was unsettled and the app could pass `color`. That risk remains. Bundling `color_option` with env detection widens scope, but together they address what users ask for.
searches: pallets click NO_COLOR FORCE_COLOR support issue

option-value-separator.who_benefits: Authors wanting `--tags a,b,c` lists. Real need, but the usual workaround is a short split callback. Env, default_map and prompt handling add scope beyond what was asked.

user_evidence.finding: Open request for a non-whitespace separator on options. Maintainers were sceptical: davidism said the parser gets pre-split tokens and showed a split callback. AndreasBackx called comma separators uncommon and confusing. The issue was removed from the 9.0.0 milestone. kdeldycke shipped MultiChoice in click-extra instead.
click-extra provides MultiChoice because click has no equivalent, which shows some demand.

contrived_rules: Help metavar '<M>[<sep><M>...]' format
Completion that re-attaches earlier segments
separator combined with multiple=True is allowed as a no-op
TypeError for is_flag/count/nargs!=1 combinations
option-value-separator.reasoning: The demand is real but modest. Maintainers have signalled reluctance and point to a callback workaround. The outline spreads across env, default_map, prompt, completion and help, which is a large surface for a niche feature. Related upstream requests (#2771) were about nargs=-1 with a separator, not this multiple-style API.
searches: click option comma separated list multiple values python stackoverflow

mutually-exclusive-params.who_benefits: CLI authors with flags such as --json/--yaml/--csv. This is a common need that is usually solved with hand-written checks or cloup. The workaround is simple, though.

user_evidence.finding: Gist with a hand-written exclusive() helper.
cloup offers mutually_exclusive as part of a constraint system.
Long-running request with 37 comments. It was closed by mitsuhiko in 2015: there is 'no likely API' and it can be checked in callbacks. He doubted useful help text could be generated.

contrived_rules: Message names only the first two explicit members in declared order
Only the first violation is reported
A false-spelling flag such as --no-json still counts as provided
PROMPT source counts as explicit but DEFAULT_MAP does not
mutually-exclusive-params.reasoning: Demand is clear. Many issues (#257, #509, #1137, #2252, #2342) were all closed, so maintainers have repeatedly declined. A simple name-group check in Command is more modest than option_group, which could make it more acceptable. Declined history lowers the score.
searches: click mutually exclusive options stackoverflow python

config-file-option.who_benefits: Authors of apps that want a --config file. Many need this, but it is a well-known recipe, and the format choice and file lookup are contested.

user_evidence.finding: Tutorial showing a hand-rolled eager --config callback filling default_map. It uses INI, not JSON, and the author says it is simple to do by hand.
Request for config file support closed. Maintainers (untitaker, davidism) said format and file handling should live in a third-party package and that click should not handle config formats.
Issues such as #971 and #386 were closed and none shows a built-in option was added.

contrived_rules: JSON-only format
A missing file at the default path is silently ignored but an explicit one errors
Recursive merge with file values winning
config-file-option.reasoning: Maintainers have explicitly declined config-format handling in core. The demand ref is an INI tutorial, so JSON-only addresses it loosely. click-extra already provides config_option.
searches: click config file option default_map callback --config python

choice-enum-by-value.who_benefits: Authors using Enum or StrEnum with Choice who want users to type values, which is common. Several users have hit this.

user_evidence.finding: Enum support was added using names because they are unique. Values were left to click-extra EnumChoice.
Many issues: #2911 'Choice prefers Enum.name even for StrEnum', #3028 prompt shows values but requires names, #2970, #2959. The EnumChoice PR #2210 was closed.

contrived_rules: Int-valued enums match on the stringified value
to_info_dict must stay unchanged
choice-enum-by-value.reasoning: Recurring user pain, with a 2025 name-vs-value confusion, and Typer defaults to values. But maintainers closed the EnumChoice PRs and may prefer a separate type. A flag on Choice is a smaller change. The multi-site help, prompt and completion changes are legitimate consistency fixes.
searches: click.Choice enum values instead of names python stackoverflow

help-styles.who_benefits: Authors who want coloured help. There is a niche audience, served by click-help-colors (92 stars), rich-click and cloup.

user_evidence.finding: Small package with 92 stars, so modest demand.
No matching upstream issues.

contrived_rules: An explicit prefix to write_usage is not restyled
Unknown keys in help_styles are silently ignored
Only 'heading' and 'term' keys
help-styles.reasoning: No upstream request was found, and the ecosystem already covers it through formatter_class. It adds a new Context setting and HelpFormatter signature, while click keeps help plain. Adoption of the existing add-ons is modest.
